flags.title: Same-day evaluation for suspected unstable angina?
flags.concern: Unstable angina is the working diagnosis, yet the plan is a cardiology visit next week and a stress test, which is usually avoided until an acute coronary syndrome is excluded. If the pattern is truly stable exertional angina (three months, relieved by rest), the label may instead overstate the urgency.
flags.consider: You might clarify whether the pattern is crescendo or at rest and, if unstable angina is still suspected, consider same-day evaluation with troponins rather than outpatient stress testing.

flags.title: Conflicting nitroglycerin and 911 instructions?
flags.concern: The patient was first told to go to the hospital if pain persists after one or two pills, then told she can take up to three pills five minutes apart, which could delay emergency care. Contraindications such as PDE5 inhibitor use, and bleeding history before aspirin, were not checked.
flags.consider: Consider giving one clear instruction (call 911 if pain is not improved five minutes after the first dose) and confirming no PDE5 inhibitor use or bleeding risk.

flags.title: Statin and lipid panel for suspected CAD?
flags.concern: A 53-year-old with diabetes, hypertension, family history and suspected coronary blockage was not started on a statin and no lipid panel was ordered.
flags.consider: You might consider checking a lipid panel and starting a high-intensity statin given her diabetes and suspected coronary disease.

flags.title: HCTZ versus ACE inhibitor/ARB in diabetes?
flags.concern: Hydrochlorothiazide was started in a patient with diabetes, partly for ankle edema, without a blood pressure reading in the visit, baseline electrolytes or renal function, urine albumin, or a sulfa allergy check; thiazides can also raise glucose.
flags.consider: Consider confirming the blood pressure, checking a BMP and urine albumin, and whether an ACE inhibitor or ARB would suit her diabetes better as first-line therapy.
